note: Pet Peeves, content v3 (25 words, 2 grammar rules). Course level B1.1 (Gateway level 9), unit Pet Peeves, from the Anki Pet-Peeves export.

words.meaning: People who tell others how to behave but don't follow their own advice.
situations: My uncle tells everyone to stop smoking, but he smokes a pack a day himself.
Our boss shouts at us for being late, then walks in at ten every morning.
gaps: I can't stand ______ who tell you to save money while they waste theirs.
Politicians who talk about saving water but fill their huge pools are ______.
Don't be one of those ______ who say 'be kind online' and then post mean comments.
hints: They say one thing and do the opposite.
Starts with 'hypo-'; the singular ends in '-crite'.

commonMistakes.correction: He is a real hypocrite.
commonMistakes.why: 'Hypocrisy' is the behaviour; the person is a 'hypocrite'.

words.meaning: Charging much higher prices than normal for things people badly need, especially during a shortage or emergency.
situations: During the storm, the shop near my house sold bottles of water for five times what they normally cost.
When everyone needed face masks, some websites sold a box for $80 instead of $5.
gaps: The store was fined for ______ after it tripled the cost of water during the flood.
Charging crazy amounts for medicine during a crisis is ______.
The government passed a law against ______ during emergencies.
hints: Raising prices unfairly when people have no choice.
Two words: 'price' + a word meaning to overcharge.

commonMistakes.sentence: The shop did a price gouge on water.
commonMistakes.correction: The shop was accused of price gouging on water.
commonMistakes.why: Use the noun phrase 'price gouging' (or the verb 'gouge customers').

words.meaning: Describes a person who gets angry very quickly, even about small things — it's part of their personality.
situations: My neighbour starts shouting the moment a child's ball touches his car — he's been like that for years.
Our old coach lost his patience with players over tiny mistakes in every single practice.
gaps: He's very ______ — he loses his patience over the smallest thing.
Don't argue with her; she's ______ and will start shouting.
Working long hours made him tired and ______.
hints: Gets angry quickly as a personality trait — the opposite of patient.
Two words with a hyphen: 'short' + a word for mood.

commonMistakes.correction: He is very short-tempered.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective ends in '-ed': short-tempered.

words.meaning: Eating without closing your lips, so other people can see the food in your mouth.
situations: At dinner, my cousin talked while eating, and everyone could see the half-eaten rice in his mouth.
My mum always tells my little brother, 'Close your lips when you eat!'
gaps: ______ is considered very rude at the table.
My biggest pet peeve at restaurants is ______ — I don't want to see your food.
Kids need to learn that ______ is bad table manners.
hints: A table-manners problem you can see, not just hear.
Starts with 'Chewing with…'.

commonMistakes.correction: He chews with his mouth open.
commonMistakes.why: Say 'with his/your mouth open' — the possessive is needed.

words.meaning: People who don't keep their body, hands or space clean.
situations: My roommate never washes his hands after the bathroom and leaves dirty plates for days.
On the hot bus, a man who clearly hadn't showered for a week sat next to me.
gaps: ______ who don't wash their hands after the bathroom really annoy me.
Sharing a kitchen with ______ is a nightmare.
The gym asked members to wipe the machines because of a few ______.
hints: People who aren't clean — the opposite of 'hygienic'.
The adjective starts with 'un-'.

commonMistakes.correction: He is an unhygienic person.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'unhygienic'; 'hygiene' is the noun.

words.meaning: Speaking to people in short, sharp, angry words, usually because you are tired or stressed.
situations: When I asked my sister a simple question this morning, she answered 'What?! I'm busy!' and turned away.
Dad didn't sleep last night, so every time we talked to him, he answered in one rude word.
gaps: She was ______ with everyone at work today because she didn't sleep well.
Sorry I was ______ on the phone — I was really stressed.
Don't be so ______ with the waiter; it's not his fault.
hints: About how you talk: quick, sharp, irritated replies.
From the verb 'snap' + '-y'.

commonMistakes.correction: She was snappy with me. / She snapped at me.
commonMistakes.why: 'Snappy' is an adjective; the verb is 'snap at someone'.

words.meaning: Workers who prepare or serve food with their bare hands instead of wearing gloves.
situations: The man at the sandwich shop took my money, then made my sandwich with the same bare hands.
At the bakery, the worker picked up my croissant with her bare fingers instead of using tongs.
gaps: ______ are one of my biggest pet peeves — it just feels unsafe.
The restaurant was fined because inspectors saw ______ touching raw meat and salad.
I stopped eating at that burger place because of the ______.
hints: Kitchen workers with no gloves on.
Starts with 'Glove-' and ends with 'handlers'.

commonMistakes.correction: The cook wasn't wearing gloves.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'gloveless' (no 's' in the middle).

words.meaning: In a bad, complaining mood — quietly annoyed and unfriendly, but not shouting.
situations: Every morning before his coffee, my dad sits at the table, frowns and complains about everything.
The old man next door never smiles and moans about the weather, the noise and the neighbours.
gaps: He's always ______ before he's had his morning coffee.
Why are you so ______ today? You haven't smiled once.
My cat gets ______ when I wake her up.
hints: A bad, complaining mood — like one of the seven dwarfs.
Rhymes with 'lumpy'.

commonMistakes.correction: He is grumpy today.
commonMistakes.why: After 'is', use the adjective 'grumpy'; 'grumpily' is an adverb.

words.meaning: To make someone very annoyed or angry (informal and a bit rude — use with friends, not at work).
situations: It really makes me mad when people take my parking spot after I've been waiting with my signal on.
My friend keeps borrowing my charger and never gives it back, and I'm sick of it.
gaps: It really ______ when people cut in line.
Stop doing that — you're going to ______!
Nothing ______ more than slow Wi-Fi.
hints: A rude informal way to say 'make someone very angry'.
Phrasal verb with 'off'; the adjective is '___ed off'.

commonMistakes.correction: He pissed me off.
commonMistakes.why: With a pronoun, it goes in the middle: piss me off.

words.meaning: People who talk during a film at the cinema and spoil it for everyone else.
situations: The couple behind us in the cinema discussed their weekend plans through the whole film.
A man in the front row kept explaining the story to his friend in a loud voice.
gaps: ______ are one of my biggest pet peeves — I paid to hear the film, not their chat.
The cinema shows a 'please be quiet' message to stop ______.
I prefer watching films at home, away from ______.
hints: Cinema-goers who chat during the film.
Two words: 'movie' + people who talk.

commonMistakes.correction: They are movie talkers.
commonMistakes.why: Use the plural 'talkers' for more than one person.

words.meaning: Sudden, uncontrolled outbursts of anger with crying, screaming or kicking — especially by young children.
situations: In the supermarket, a little boy lay on the floor, screaming and kicking because his mum said no to sweets.
My two-year-old niece cries and bangs her fists on the floor every time we turn off the TV.
gaps: Toddlers often have ______ when they're tired or hungry.
His ______ in the toy shop embarrassed his parents.
Parents need patience to deal with a child's ______.
hints: The noun: a child's screaming, kicking outbursts.
Two words: 'temper' + a word starting with 't'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The child did a temper tantrum.
commonMistakes.correction: The child threw / had a temper tantrum.
commonMistakes.why: We 'throw' or 'have' a tantrum, not 'do' one.

words.meaning: Speakers playing music or sound extremely loudly, in an unpleasant way.
situations: The neighbours played music so loud last night that my windows were shaking until 3 a.m.
On the beach, a group of teenagers turned their music up so high that nobody could talk.
gaps: The neighbour's ______ kept me awake until 3 a.m.
I can't study with those ______ next door.
The café had ______, so we couldn't hear each other.
hints: Very loud speakers that annoy everyone.
Two words: an adjective meaning 'very loud' + 'speakers'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The speakers were blaming all night.
commonMistakes.correction: The speakers were blaring all night.
commonMistakes.why: The verb is 'blare' (be very loud), not 'blame'.

words.meaning: To say or do something on purpose to make someone angry or get a strong reaction.
situations: My little brother kept poking me and saying 'you can't catch me' just to make me lose my temper.
Some online commenters write insulting things on purpose so people will argue with them.
gaps: Don't ______ him — you know he gets angry easily.
She said it just to ______ a reaction.
The player was sent off for trying to ______ the other team.
hints: Annoy someone on purpose to get a reaction.
Starts with 'pro-' and rhymes with 'joke'.

commonMistakes.correction: He provoked me. / He made me angry.
commonMistakes.why: 'Provoke someone' — don't add 'to angry'.

words.meaning: Feeling annoyed, usually because something small keeps happening again and again.
situations: The man next to me on the plane kept tapping his pen, and after an hour I was ready to scream.
The phone kept buzzing with ads all morning, and Sara was getting more and more annoyed.
gaps: She was ______ by the constant noise from the building site.
I get ______ when people don't reply to my messages.
He looked ______ when his phone rang for the fifth time.
hints: How you feel when small things keep annoying you.
The '-ed' adjective from 'irritate'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I'm very irritating by the noise.
commonMistakes.correction: I'm very irritated by the noise.
commonMistakes.why: Use '-ed' for how you feel (irritated); '-ing' for the thing that causes it (irritating).

words.meaning: To suddenly start screaming, crying or kicking because you're angry and can't get what you want.
situations: When the shop assistant said the toy was sold out, the boy started screaming and kicking the shelves.
My manager slammed his laptop shut and shouted when the meeting didn't go his way.
gaps: The child began to ______ because he wanted a toy.
Don't ______ just because you lost the game!
My little sister will ______ if we don't let her come.
hints: The verb phrase: start an angry outburst like a child.
Three words: '___ a tantrum'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He made a tantrum in the shop.
commonMistakes.correction: He threw a tantrum in the shop.
commonMistakes.why: The verb that goes with 'tantrum' is 'throw'.

words.meaning: Eating food in a way that makes loud, unpleasant chewing noises.
situations: In the quiet office, my co-worker eats crisps and apples, and everyone can hear every crunch.
At the cinema, the man next to me ate his popcorn so noisily that I couldn't hear the film.
gaps: His ______ at the dinner table really bothers me.
______ in a quiet office is so annoying.
My biggest pet peeve is ______ — I can hear every bite.
hints: A noisy eating habit you hear, not see.
Two words: an '-ing' eating verb + an adverb.

commonMistakes.correction: He chews loudly.
commonMistakes.why: Use the adverb 'loudly' to describe how he chews.

words.meaning: Making a loud sucking noise while drinking or eating something wet, like soup or tea.
situations: My uncle drinks his hot tea with a long, loud 'sssp' sound from the cup.
At the noodle bar, the man next to me sucked up his soup so noisily that people turned around.
gaps: His ______ while drinking soup is one of my biggest pet peeves.
Stop ______ your milkshake — it's so loud!
In some countries, ______ noodles is polite.
hints: The noise of sucking up a drink or soup.
Starts with 'slur-' and ends in '-ing'.

commonMistakes.correction: He slurped his soup loudly.
commonMistakes.why: Put the object after 'slurp' and the adverb at the end.

words.meaning: To go in front of people who are already waiting, without asking — often sneakily.
situations: We'd waited 20 minutes for coffee when a woman walked past us and stood right at the front.
At the bus stop, a man quietly slipped in front of an old lady when the bus arrived.
gaps: I hate it when people ______ at the grocery store.
Hey! Don't ______ — we've all been waiting!
He tried to ______ by pretending he knew someone at the front.
hints: Go in front of people waiting, without pushing.
Three words: '___ in line'.

commonMistakes.sentence: She cut the line in front of me.
commonMistakes.correction: She cut in line in front of me.
commonMistakes.why: The phrase is 'cut in line' (or 'jump the queue' in British English).

words.meaning: To push other people roughly with your body to get ahead of them in a queue.
situations: When the shop doors opened, a big man used his elbows to push everyone and get to the front.
At the concert gate, people were pushing others so hard that a girl almost fell.
gaps: When the doors opened, people started to ______ and someone fell.
Please don't ______ — there's enough food for everyone.
The kids began to ______ to be first on the bus.
hints: Push people physically to get ahead in a queue.
Three words: a verb meaning 'push hard' + 'in line'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He shoved me in line to get first.
commonMistakes.correction: He shoved in line to get to the front.
commonMistakes.why: 'Shove in line' means pushing ahead; 'shove someone' means pushing a person.

collocations: shove your way to the front

words.meaning: When a boss controls and checks every tiny detail of your work instead of trusting you to do it.
situations: My boss checks every email I write before I send it and asks for updates every 30 minutes.
The manager told the designer exactly which font, colour and size to use for every single word.
gaps: My boss's ______ makes it hard for me to work on my own.
Good managers avoid ______ and trust their team.
Constant ______ makes employees feel stressed and useless.
hints: A boss controlling every small detail.
Starts with 'micro-' and ends with '-ment'.

commonMistakes.correction: My boss micromanages everything.
commonMistakes.why: The verb is 'micromanage'; 'micromanagement' is the noun.

words.meaning: To move to one side so someone can pass; also, to leave your job or position so someone else can take it.
situations: Two people stood chatting in the middle of the narrow shop aisle, and I had to ask them to move so I could get past.
After 20 years, the old manager left his position so a younger person could lead the company.
gaps: I wish people would ______ instead of blocking the whole aisle.
Could you ______, please? I need to get through.
The CEO decided to ______ and let her deputy take over.
hints: Move out of the way — or give your job to someone else.
Two words: 'step' + a word meaning 'to one side'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Please step aside of the door.
commonMistakes.correction: Please step aside from the door. / Please step aside.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'step aside' alone, or 'step aside from' — not 'of'.

words.meaning: To make yourself do something unpleasant or difficult that you've been avoiding.
situations: Omar was scared of the dentist for months, but today he finally booked an appointment.
Sara hated asking her boss for a raise, but she took a deep breath and knocked on his door.
gaps: My tooth hurt so much that I had to ______ and go to the dentist.
I've been avoiding the exam, but it's time to ______ and start studying.
He decided to ______ and tell his parents the truth.
hints: Finally do the hard thing you've been avoiding.
Idiom with a gun word: '___ the bullet'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I bit a bullet and called her.
commonMistakes.correction: I bit the bullet and called her.
commonMistakes.why: The fixed idiom is 'bite the bullet' — with 'the'.

collocations: bite the bullet and do something

words.meaning: Complaining angrily and loudly about something for a long time, usually without doing anything to fix it.
situations: My uncle spent the whole family dinner complaining loudly about the government, but he's never voted.
For an hour, my roommate shouted about the noisy neighbours instead of just knocking on their door.
gaps: Stop ______ about the problem and try to find a solution.
He was ______ about the bad service for the whole evening.
She came home ______ about her boss again.
hints: Two '-ing' words joined by 'and' — angry, long complaining.
R___ing and r___ing.

commonMistakes.correction: He was ranting and raving.
commonMistakes.why: The fixed order is 'ranting and raving'.

words.meaning: A casual way to say that you're not doing well, or that something is old and in bad condition.
situations: When her friend asked how she was, Mona sighed and said things weren't great — she'd lost her job.
My grandad's old car is rusty, the door won't close and the radio doesn't work anymore.
gaps: A: How are you doing? B: Honestly, ______.
This old sofa has ______ — look at the holes.
After the flu, I can only say ______.
hints: A casual way to say 'I'm not okay'.
Starts with 'I've seen…'.

commonMistakes.correction: I've seen better days.
commonMistakes.why: The fixed expression uses the present perfect: I've seen.

words.meaning: To suddenly start shouting angrily at a particular person.
situations: When I arrived five minutes late, my boss started shouting at me in front of everyone.
The customer suddenly began yelling at the young waiter because his food was cold.
gaps: My boss started to ______ me for being five minutes late.
Don't ______ the waiter — it's not his fault.
She'll ______ you if you're late again.
hints: Suddenly shout angrily at someone.
A three-word phrasal verb starting with 'go'.

commonMistakes.correction: He went off on me.
commonMistakes.why: The phrasal verb is 'go off on someone'.

grammar.rule: Either/Or, Neither/Nor, Not only/But also Paired conjunctions
grammar.explanation: Either…or = a choice between two things. Neither…nor = not this and not that (the verb is positive). Not only…but also = adds more; at the start of a sentence, 'not only' is followed by question order (Not only was she…).
examples: You can either eat pasta or pizza.
I like neither coffee nor tea.
Not only was the girl smart, but she was also beautiful.

commonMistakes.sentence: I don't like neither coffee nor tea.
commonMistakes.correction: I like neither coffee nor tea.
commonMistakes.why: 'Neither…nor' is already negative — don't add 'don't'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Not only she was smart, but she was also kind.
commonMistakes.correction: Not only was she smart, but she was also kind.
commonMistakes.why: After 'Not only' at the start, use question order: was she.

questions.prompt: You can ______ stay at home or come with us.

options: Not only was he rude, but he was also late.
Not only he was rude, but he was also late.
questions.answer: Not only was he rude, but he was also late.
questions.explanation: After 'Not only' at the start of a sentence, use question order.

questions.sentence: I don't want neither pizza nor pasta.
questions.fix: I want neither pizza nor pasta.

questions.sentence: She is not only smart but also she is kind.
questions.answer: She is not only smart but also kind.
questions.explanation: Put the same kind of word after 'not only' and 'but also' (smart / kind).

grammar.explanation: 'What … for?' asks why someone did something. It's casual; 'why' is more neutral. Put 'what' at the start and 'for' at the very end.
examples: What did you call him for? (= Why did you call him?)
What did you go there alone for?

commonMistakes.sentence: What for did you call him?
commonMistakes.correction: What did you call him for?
commonMistakes.why: 'For' goes at the end of the question.

commonMistakes.correction: What did you call him for?
commonMistakes.why: Use question order with an auxiliary: did you call.

questions.prompt: Which question means 'Why did you buy that?'
options: What did you buy that for?
What for did you buy that?
What did you buy for that?
questions.answer: What did you buy that for?
questions.explanation: What + question + for at the end.
'… for?' at the end pairs with 'What' at the start.

questions.sentence: What did you go there alone for?
questions.alternative: What you went there alone for?
questions.explanation: Correct: question order + 'for' at the end.

questions.answer: What did you call her for?
questions.explanation: Use question order: did you call.
